scenes.narration: Between the birth and the legend of Woodrow Wilson lie the years that actually decide it. Thomas Woodrow Wilson (December 28, 1856 – February 3, 1924) was the 28th president of the United States, serving from 1913 to 1921. He was the only Democrat to serve as president during the Progressive Era, when Republicans dominated the presidency and legislative branches.

The reputation of Woodrow Wilson was built in the middle, not at the edges. As president, Wilson made significant economic reforms and led the United States through World War I. He was the leading architect of the League of Nations, and his stance on foreign policy came to be known as Wilsonian idealism.

Somebody like Woodrow Wilson should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Born in Staunton, Virginia, Wilson grew up in the Southern United States during the American Civil War and Reconstruction era. After earning a PhD in history and political science from Johns Hopkins University, Wilson taught at several colleges prior to being appointed president of Princeton University, where he emerged as a prominent spokesman for progressivism in higher education.

The life of Woodrow Wilson begins far from where the story usually starts. Wilson is considered one of the founding fathers of the field of public administration due to his 1887 article "The Study of Administration". Wilson served as the governor of New Jersey from 1911 to 1913, during which he broke with party bosses and won the passage of several progressive reforms.

Woodrow Wilson was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In the 1912 election, Wilson defeated the incumbent Republican president, William Howard Taft, and the third-party nominee and former president Theodore Roosevelt, becoming the first Southerner to win the presidency since Zachary Taylor in the 1848 election. During his first year as president, Wilson authorized the widespread imposition of racial segregation inside the federal bureaucracy, and his opposition to women's suffrage drew protests.

To understand where Woodrow Wilson ended up, start with where Woodrow Wilson began. His first term was largely devoted to pursuing the passage of his progressive New Freedom domestic agenda. His first major priority was the Revenue Act of 1913, which began the modern income tax, and the Federal Reserve Act, which created the Federal Reserve System.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Woodrow Wilson ran through years nobody filmed. At the outbreak of World War I in 1914, the U.S. declared neutrality as Wilson tried to negotiate peace between the Allied and Central Powers. Wilson was narrowly re-elected in the 1916 election, defeating Republican nominee Charles Evans Hughes.

Each stage of the life of Woodrow Wilson made the next stage possible. In April 1917, Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war against Germany in response to its policy of unrestricted submarine warfare that sank American merchant ships. Wilson concentrated on diplomacy, issuing the Fourteen Points that the Allies and Germany accepted as a basis for post-war peace.

The people who knew Woodrow Wilson young describe someone already restless. He wanted the off-year elections of 1918 to be a referendum endorsing his policies but instead the Republicans took control of Congress. After the Allied victory in November 1918, Wilson attended the Paris Peace Conference.

What Woodrow Wilson built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Wilson had intended to seek a third term in office but had a stroke in October 1919 that left him incapacitated. Meanwhile, his policies alienated German- and Irish-American Democrats and the Republicans won a landslide in the 1920 election.

By the time Woodrow Wilson reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Into the 21st century, historians have criticized Wilson for supporting racial segregation, although they continue to rank Wilson as an above-average president for his accomplishments in office. Conservatives in particular have criticized him for expanding the federal government, while others have praised him decreasing the power of large corporations and have credited him for establishing modern liberalism.

The rise of Woodrow Wilson was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born to a family of Scotch-Irish and Scottish descent in Staunton, Virginia. He was the third of four children and the first son of Joseph Ruggles Wilson and Jessie Janet Woodrow.

Setbacks came early for Woodrow Wilson, and the response to them is the real story. Wilson's paternal grandparents had immigrated to the United States from Strabane, County Tyrone, Ireland, in 1807, and settled in Steubenville, Ohio. Wilson's paternal grandfather James Wilson published a pro-tariff and anti-slavery newspaper, The Western Herald and Gazette.

The legacy of Woodrow Wilson outlived the circumstances that produced it. Wilson's maternal grandfather, the Reverend Thomas Woodrow, moved from Paisley, Renfrewshire, Scotland, to Carlisle, Cumbria, England, before migrating to Chillicothe, Ohio, in the late 1830s. Joseph met Jessie while she was attending a girls' academy in Steubenville, and the two married on June 7, 1849.

Few lives travel as far as that of Woodrow Wilson, and the distance is the point. Soon after the wedding, Joseph was ordained as a Presbyterian pastor and assigned to serve in Staunton. His son Woodrow was born in the Manse, a house in the Staunton First Presbyterian Church where Joseph served.

The childhood of Woodrow Wilson contains the adult in small print. Before he was two years old, the family moved to Augusta, Georgia. Wilson was one of only two U.S. presidents to be a citizen of the Confederate States of America; the other was John Tyler, who served as the nation's tenth president from 1841 to 1845.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Woodrow Wilson — in that order. Wilson's father identified with the Southern United States and was a staunch supporter of the Confederacy during the American Civil War. Wilson's father was one of the founders of the Presbyterian Church in the Confederate States of America, later renamed the Presbyterian Church in the United States (PCUS), following its 1861 split from the Northern Presbyterians.

The turning point in the life of Woodrow Wilson looked like a failure at the time. He became minister of the First Presbyterian Church in Augusta, and the family lived there until 1870. From 1870 to 1874, Wilson lived in Columbia, South Carolina, where his father was a theology professor at the Columbia Theological Seminary.

Every biography of Woodrow Wilson has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In 1873, Wilson became a communicant member of the Columbia First Presbyterian Church; he remained a member throughout his life. He was also elected secretary of the school's football association, president of the school's baseball association, and managing editor of the student newspaper.

The education of Woodrow Wilson happened mostly outside any school. In the hotly contested presidential election of 1876, Wilson supported the Democratic Party and its nominee, Samuel J. After graduating from Princeton in 1879, Wilson attended the University of Virginia School of Law in Charlottesville, Virginia, where he was involved in the Virginia Glee Club and served as president of the Jefferson Literary and Debating Society.

What Woodrow Wilson wanted at the start and what Woodrow Wilson got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Poor health forced Wilson to withdraw from law school, but he continued to study law on his own while living with his parents in Wilmington, North Carolina. Wilson was admitted to the Georgia bar and made a brief attempt at establishing a law firm in Atlanta in 1882.

The defining trait of Woodrow Wilson was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Though he found legal history and substantive jurisprudence interesting, he abhorred the day-to-day procedural aspects of the practice of law. After less than a year, Wilson abandoned his legal practice to pursue the study of political science and history.

Those who met Woodrow Wilson at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. In late 1883, Wilson enrolled at the recently established Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore for doctoral studies in history, political science, German, and other fields. Wilson spent much of his time at Johns Hopkins University writing Congressional Government: A Study in American Politics, which grew out of a series of essays in which he examined the workings of the federal government.

The private years of Woodrow Wilson explain the public decades better than any speech. In 1886, Wilson was awarded a Ph.D. in history and government from Johns Hopkins University, making him the only U.S. president in the nation's history to possess a Ph.D. In 1883, Wilson met and fell in love with Ellen Louise Axson.

The family Woodrow Wilson came from matters more than the legends admit. He proposed marriage in September 1883; she accepted, but they agreed to postpone marriage while Wilson attended graduate school. Axson graduated from Art Students League of New York, worked in portraiture, and received a medal for one of her works from the Exposition Universelle (1878) in Paris.

The first real success of Woodrow Wilson arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Ellen learned German so she could help translate German-language political science publications relevant to Woodrow's research. In 1913, Jessie married Francis Bowes Sayre Sr., who later served as High Commissioner to the Philippines.

The last chapter of Woodrow Wilson was written long after the fame. In 1914, their third child Eleanor married William Gibbs McAdoo, U.S. secretary of the treasury under Woodrow Wilson and later a U.S. senator from California. From 1885 to 1888, Wilson taught at Bryn Mawr College, a newly established women's college in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania, outside Philadelphia.

The whole life of Woodrow Wilson reads like a single decision repeated. Wilson taught ancient Greek and Roman history, American history, political science, and other subjects. During this time, Wilson's 1887 journal article "The Study of Administration" was published in Political Science Quarterly.

Between the birth and the legend of Woodrow Wilson lie the years that actually decide it. It argued that public administration should be considered its own field of study instead of a sub-field of political science, and that administrators should be separate but accountable to political leaders, who in turn are accountable to the people. The article is widely considered foundational in the field of public administration, and Wilson is credited as one of the field's founding fathers.

The reputation of Woodrow Wilson was built in the middle, not at the edges. Wilson's essay was influenced by Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel's treatment of law and the state in Elements of the Philosophy of Right, especially Hegel's picture of how public institutions arise and mediate social conflict. Wilson accepted a position at Wesleyan University, an undergraduate college for men in Middletown, Connecticut.

Somebody like Woodrow Wilson should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. He taught graduate courses in political economy and Western history, coached Wesleyan's football team, and founded a debate team. In February 1890, with the help of friends, Wilson was appointed Chair of Jurisprudence and Political Economy at the College of New Jersey (the name at the time of Princeton University), at an annual salary of $3,000 (equivalent to $107,500 in 2025).

The life of Woodrow Wilson begins far from where the story usually starts. In 1896, Francis Landey Patton announced that College of New Jersey was being renamed Princeton University; an ambitious program of expansion for the university accompanied the name change. In the 1896 presidential election, Wilson rejected Democratic nominee William Jennings Bryan as too far to the left and instead supported the conservative "Gold Democrat" nominee, John M.

Wilson's academic reputation continued to grow throughout the 1890s, and he turned down multiple positions elsewhere, including at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Virginia. At Princeton University, Wilson published several works of history and political science and was a regular contributor to Political Science Quarterly.
